About reaction-diffusion systems involving the Holling-type II and the Beddington-DeAngelis functional responses for predator-prey models

F. CONFORTO11 1 Dipartimento di Scienze Matematiche e Informatiche, Scienze Fisiche e Scienze della Terra, Università di Messina, Viale Stagno d’Alcontres 31, 98166 Messina, Italy, L. DESVILLETTES22 2 Université Paris Diderot, Sorbonne Paris Cité, Institut de Mathématiques de Jussieu-Paris Rive Gauche, UMR 7586, CNRS, Sorbonne Universités, UPMC Univ. Paris 06, F-75013, Paris, France, AND C. SORESINA33 3 Centro de Matemática, Aplicações Fundamentais e Investigação Operacional, Universidade de Lisboa, Faculty of Science, Campo Grande, 1749-016 Lisboa, Portugal

Keywords: Cross diffusion equations, predator-prey equations, Turing instability, Turing patterns, functional responses

AMS Classification: 35B25, 35B36, 35K45, 35K57, 35Q92, 92D25

Abstract

We consider in this paper a microscopic model (that is, a system of three reaction-diffusion equations) incorporating the dynamics of handling and searching predators, and show that its solutions converge when a small parameter tends to 00 towards the solutions of a reaction-cross diffusion system of predator-prey type involving a Holling-type II or Beddington-DeAngelis functional response. We also provide a study of the Turing instability domain of the obtained equations and (in the case of the Beddington-DeAngelis functional response) compare it to the same instability domain when the cross diffusion is replaced by a standard diffusion.

1 Introduction

1.1 General presentation

Complex functional responses are widely used in predator-prey models [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. For example, the Holling-type II functional response [1] is based on the idea that predators will catch a limited proportion of available prey in the case when preys are abundant. Denoting with N:=N⁡(t)N:=N(t) the prey biomass, and with P:=P⁡(t)P:=P(t) the predator biomass, this type of functional response leads to the following set of two ODEs:

N˙=r0​g​(N)−b​N​P1+k​N,P˙=c​b​N​P1+k​N−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dot{N}&=r_{0}g(N)-\dfrac{bNP}{1+kN},\\ \dot{P}&=\dfrac{cbNP}{1+kN}-\mu P,\end{split} (1)

where r0,b,c,k,μ>0r_{0},\;b,\;c,\;k,\;\mu>0, and where the function gg describes the prey growth and can be either linear, that is g⁡(N)=Ng(N)=N, or involve a logistic part as g⁡(N)=(1−η​N)​Ng(N)=(1-\eta N)N with η>0\eta>0 [6]. Note that when g⁡(N)=Ng(N)=N and k=0k=0, one recovers the classical Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model.

If one also wishes to take into account the competition between predators when they try to catch prey, the slightly more complex Beddington-DeAngelis functional response can be introduced [3, 4]:

N˙=r0​g​(N)−b​N​P1+k​N+h​P,P˙=c​b​N​P1+k​N+h​P−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dot{N}&=r_{0}g(N)-\dfrac{bNP}{1+kN+hP},\\ \dot{P}&=\dfrac{cbNP}{1+kN+hP}-\mu P,\end{split} (2)

where r0,b,c,k,h>0r_{0},\;b,\;c,\;k,\;h>0.

An important point in the sequel will be the observation that predator-prey models with the Beddington-DeAngelis functional response are known to produce patterns (coming out of a Turing instability) when diffusion terms with suitable rates (denotes by dN,dPd_{N},\;d_{P}) are added to the reaction term [7, 8]. In such a situation, the system becomes:

∂tN−dN​Δx​N=r0​g​(N)−b​N​P1+k​N+h​P,∂tP−dP​Δx​P=c​b​N​P1+k​N+h​P−μ​P.\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{t}N-d_{N}\Delta_{x}N&=r_{0}g(N)-\dfrac{bNP}{1+kN+hP},\\ \partial_{t}P-d_{P}\Delta_{x}P&=\dfrac{cbNP}{1+kN+hP}-\mu P.\end{split} (3)

On the other hand, no patterns are known to appear in the case of a reaction-diffusion predator-prey model with a Holling-type II functional response and diffusion terms as in (3) [9] (patterns may however appear when richer dynamics are considered, for example when one adds quadratic intra-predator interaction or fighting term [10, 11], or a density-dependent predator mortality [11]). In all these cases, a fundamental assumption is that the diffusion coefficients of the two species must be different; patterns appearing taking equal diffusion coefficient are studied in [12, 13, 14]).

Several works were written in the past in order to obtain a derivation of the Holling-type II and Beddington-DeAngelis functional responses out of simple and realistic “microscopic models” which in some limit lead, at least formally, to (1) or (2). Such a model was designed by Metz and Diekmann [15] for the Holling-type II functional response, and by Geritz and Gyllenberg [16], Huisman and De Boer [17], for the Beddington-DeAngelis one, and references therein.

Metz and Diekmann proposed a system of three ODEs, in which the predators are divided in two classes (respectively called searching and handling), while the interaction between predators and preys is treated in a quite simple way (standard Lotka-Volterra terms are used). Predators which are searching for preys become handling with a rate proportional to the number of preys and come back to the searching state with a constant rate. Only handling predators contribute to the reproduction (and give birth to a searching predator), while the mortality rate (in absence of prey) is constant and equal for the two classes. The searching-handling switch is supposed to happen on a much faster time scale than the reproduction and mortality processes. The corresponding parameter in the system of ODEs is therefore called 1/ε1/\varepsilon, and the system writes (for some r0r_{0}, α\alpha, γ~\tilde{\gamma}, Γ\Gamma, μ\mu, ε>0\varepsilon>0)

N˙ε=r0​Nε−α​Nε​psε,p˙sε=1ε​(−α​Nε​psε+γ~​phε)+Γ​phε−μ​psε,p˙hε=1ε​(α​Nε​psε−γ~​phε)−μ​phε,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dot{N}^{\varepsilon}&=r_{0}N^{\varepsilon}-\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon},\\ \dot{p}_{s}^{\varepsilon}&=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(-\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}+\tilde{\gamma}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\right)+\Gamma p_{h}^{\varepsilon}-\mu p_{s}^{\varepsilon},\\ \dot{p}_{h}^{\varepsilon}&=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}-\tilde{\gamma}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\right)-\mu p_{h}^{\varepsilon},\end{split} (4)

where NεN^{\varepsilon} still is the density of preys, while phεp_{h}^{\varepsilon} and psεp_{s}^{\varepsilon} are the respective densities of handling and searching predators. It is shown that in the formal limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, one gets Nε→NN^{\varepsilon}\to N and psε+phε→Pp_{s}^{\varepsilon}+p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\to P where N,PN,\;P satisfy (1) (with g⁡(N):=Ng(N):=N, b:=α,k:=α/γ~,c:=Γ/γ~b:=\alpha,\;k:=\alpha/\tilde{\gamma},\;c:=\Gamma/\tilde{\gamma}) [15].

A similar procedure was later applied by Geritz and Gyllenberg in a more complex situation [16]: they divided not only the predator population into searchers and handlers, but also structured the prey population into two classes, the class of active preys (typically foraging) and prone to predation, and the class of those prey individuals who have found a refuge and cannot be caught by predators. In this way, they derived the Beddington-DeAngelis functional response in terms of mechanisms at the individual level avoiding the usual interference between predators. Previously, Huisman and De Boer [17], starting from a different four-dimensional model also obtained a system of two ordinary differential equations (they however simplified a complicated quadratic expression with a Padé approximation to recover the standard formula of the Beddington-DeAngelis functional response). In both cases, two different time scales were exploited.

We are interested in this paper in the introduction of diffusion processes in the asymptotic problem (4). Denoting by d1,d2,d3>0d_{1},\;d_{2},\;d_{3}>0 the diffusion rates of preys, searching predators and handling predators respectively, one can write, keeping the reaction term of (4), the following reaction-diffusion system:

∂tNε−d1​Δx​Nε=r0​(1−η​Nε)​Nε−α​Nε​psε,∂tpsε−d2​Δx​psε=1ε​(−α​Nε​psε+γ~​phε)+Γ​phε−μ​psε,∂tphε−d3​Δx​phε=1ε​(α​Nε​psε−γ~​phε)−μ​phε.\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{t}N^{\varepsilon}-d_{1}\Delta_{x}N^{\varepsilon}&=r_{0}\left(1-\eta N^{\varepsilon}\right)N^{\varepsilon}-\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon},\\ \partial_{t}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}-d_{2}\Delta_{x}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}&=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(-\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}+\tilde{\gamma}\,p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\right)+\Gamma p_{h}^{\varepsilon}-\mu p_{s}^{\varepsilon},\\ \partial_{t}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}-d_{3}\Delta_{x}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}&=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}-\tilde{\gamma}\,p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\right)-\mu p_{h}^{\varepsilon}.\end{split} (5)

Note that we systematically expect the diffusion rate d3d_{3} of handling predators to be smaller than the diffusion rate of searching predators d2d_{2}. The formal limit of this system when ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 is the set of two reaction cross-diffusion equations:

∂tN−d1​Δx​N=r0​(1−η​N)​N−γ~​α​Nα​N+γ~​P,∂tP−Δx​(d2​γ~+d3​α​Nα​N+γ~​P)=Γ​α​N​Pα​N+γ~−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{t}&N-d_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r_{0}(1-\eta N)N-\frac{\tilde{\gamma}\alpha N}{\alpha N+\tilde{\gamma}}P,\\ \partial_{t}&P-\Delta_{x}\bigg(\frac{d_{2}\tilde{\gamma}+d_{3}\alpha N}{\alpha N+\tilde{\gamma}}\,P\bigg)=\Gamma\frac{\alpha N\,P}{\alpha N+\tilde{\gamma}}-\mu P,\end{split} (6)

in which the reaction terms are identical (up to the change of name of the constant parameters) to those of (1), but in which the diffusion term relative to predators is much more complicated than a constant times Laplacian of PP (terms like d​Δx​Pd\Delta_{x}P will be systematically called linear diffusive terms in the sequel, while cross diffusion refers to terms like Δx​(f​(N,P)​P)\Delta_{x}(f(N,P)\,P), where ff is a smooth non-constant function of N,PN,\>P, as in the second equation of (6)). It can be noticed that the resulting cross-diffusion term is a convex combination of the diffusion coefficients d2d_{2} and d3d_{3} of the microscopic system. In Subsection 1.2 of the Introduction of this paper, we state a rigorous theorem showing that convergence of solutions to system (5) towards solutions to system (6) indeed holds when suitable functional spaces are introduced.

The same procedure can be applied in the case of Beddington-DeAngelis like functional response, that is a system of ODEs close to (2). First, we introduce a system of three ordinary differential equations modeling the interaction between preys, handling and searching predators as in (5), but in which we also take into account the competition among predators when they look for preys. This is done thanks to the introduction of the denominator 1+ξ​ps1+\xi p_{s}, for some ξ>0\xi>0, in the interaction term between predators and preys. The system writes as follows:

N˙ε=r0​(1−η​Nε)​Nε−α​Nε​psε1+ξ​psε,p˙sε=1ε​(−α​Nε​psε1+ξ​psε+γ~​phε)+Γ​phε−μ​psε,p˙hε=1ε​(α​Nε​psε1+ξ​psε−γ~​phε)−μ​phε.\displaystyle\begin{split}\dot{N}^{\varepsilon}&=r_{0}(1-\eta N^{\varepsilon})N^{\varepsilon}-\dfrac{\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}{1+\xi p_{s}^{\varepsilon}},\\ \dot{p}_{s}^{\varepsilon}&=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(-\dfrac{\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}{1+\xi p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}+\tilde{\gamma}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\right)+\Gamma p_{h}^{\varepsilon}-\mu p_{s}^{\varepsilon},\\ \dot{p}_{h}^{\varepsilon}&=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(\dfrac{\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}{1+\xi p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}-\tilde{\gamma}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\right)-\mu p_{h}^{\varepsilon}.\end{split} (7)

Its formal limit when ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 is then a system close to (2), also obtained in [17] starting from a system of four ODEs in which all interactions are linear/quadratic.

A reaction-diffusion system corresponding to (7), where the diffusion of preys, searching predators, and handling predators is taken into account through diffusion rates d1,d2,d3>0d_{1},\;d_{2},\;d_{3}>0, writes:

∂tNε−d1​Δx​Nε=r0​(1−η​Nε)​Nε−α​Nε​psε1+ξ​psε,∂tpsε−d2​Δx​psε=1ε​(−α​Nε​psε1+ξ​psε+γ~​phε)+Γ​phε−μ​psε,∂tphε−d3​Δx​phε=−1ε​(−α​Nε​psε1+ξ​psε+γ~​phε)−μ​phε.\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{t}N^{\varepsilon}-d_{1}\Delta_{x}N^{\varepsilon}&=r_{0}\left(1-\eta N^{\varepsilon}\right)N^{\varepsilon}-\dfrac{\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}{1+\xi p_{s}^{\varepsilon}},\\ \partial_{t}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}-d_{2}\Delta_{x}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}&=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\bigg(-\frac{\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}{1+\xi p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}+\tilde{\gamma}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\bigg)+\Gamma p_{h}^{\varepsilon}-\mu p_{s}^{\varepsilon},\\ \partial_{t}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}-d_{3}\Delta_{x}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}&=-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\bigg(-\frac{\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}{1+\xi p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}+\tilde{\gamma}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\bigg)-\mu p_{h}^{\varepsilon}.\end{split} (8)

We present in Subsection 1.2 of the Introduction a rigorous result of convergence of the solutions to this system towards the solution of a reaction-cross diffusion system where the reaction part is close to (2). This system writes

∂N∂T−d1​Δx​N=r⁡(1−η​N)​N−2​α​γ~​N​Pγ~+α​N+γ~​ξ​P+(γ~+α​N−γ~​ξ​P)2+4​γ~​2​ξ​P,∂P∂T−Δx​(f⁡(N,P)​P)=2​α​Γ​N​Pγ~+α​N+γ~​ξ​P+(γ~+α​N−γ~​ξ​P)2+4​γ~​2​ξ​P−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dfrac{\partial N}{\partial T}&-d_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r\left(1-\eta\,N\right)N-\dfrac{2\alpha\tilde{\gamma}NP}{\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N+\tilde{\gamma}\xi P+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N-\tilde{\gamma}\xi P)^{2}+4\tilde{\gamma}2\,\xi P}},\\ \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial T}&-\Delta_{x}\left(f(N,P)P\right)=\dfrac{2\alpha\Gamma NP}{\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N+\tilde{\gamma}\xi P+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N-\tilde{\gamma}\xi P)^{2}+4\tilde{\gamma}2\,\xi P}}-\mu P,\end{split} (9)

where

f⁡(N,P)=d2​2​γ~γ~+α​N−γ~​ξ​P+(γ~+α​N−γ~​ξ​P)2+4​γ~​2​ξ​P+d3​2​α​Nγ~+α​N+γ~​ξ​P+(γ~+α​N−γ~​ξ​P)2+4​γ~​2​ξ​P.f(N,P)=d_{2}\dfrac{2\tilde{\gamma}}{\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N-\tilde{\gamma}\xi P+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N-\tilde{\gamma}\xi P)^{2}+4\tilde{\gamma}2\,\xi P}}\\ +d_{3}\dfrac{2\alpha N}{\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N+\tilde{\gamma}\xi P+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N-\tilde{\gamma}\xi P)^{2}+4\tilde{\gamma}2\,\xi P}}. (10)

The proof of this result as well as the proof of the theorem corresponding to the Holling-type II functional response, is based on estimates coming out of two classes of methods. On one hand, we use the duality lemmas devised for reaction-diffusion systems by M. Pierre and D. Schmitt [18]. More precisely, we use an improved version of those lemmas allowing to recover LpL^{p} bounds for p>2p>2 for the solutions of such systems [19, 20]. On the other hand, we also use entropy-like functionals which are strongly reminiscent of those used in works in which microscopic models for the Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto system [21] are studied [22].

These proofs can also be compared to recent results in which reaction-cross diffusion systems are obtained as limits of standard reaction-diffusion systems with more equations, in the context of chemistry or biology [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31].

As already mentioned, the Beddington-DeAngelis like functional response is particularly interesting since it is known that predator-dependent functional responses can lead to patterns when (linear) diffusion terms are added to the reaction terms, like for example in the following system (with reaction terms identical to those in (9)):

∂N∂T−D1​Δx​N=r⁡(1−η​N)​N−2​α​γ~​N​Pγ~+α​N+γ~​ξ​P+(γ~+α​N−γ~​ξ​P)2+4​γ~​2​ξ​P,∂P∂T−D​Δx​P=2​α​Γ​N​Pγ~+α​N+γ~​ξ​P+(γ~+α​N−γ~​ξ​P)2+4​γ~​2​ξ​P−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dfrac{\partial N}{\partial T}&-D_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r\left(1-\eta\,N\right)N-\dfrac{2\alpha\tilde{\gamma}NP}{\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N+\tilde{\gamma}\xi P+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N-\tilde{\gamma}\xi P)^{2}+4\tilde{\gamma}2\,\xi P}},\\ \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial T}&-D\Delta_{x}P=\dfrac{2\alpha\Gamma NP}{\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N+\tilde{\gamma}\xi P+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha N-\tilde{\gamma}\xi P)^{2}+4\tilde{\gamma}2\,\xi P}}-\mu P,\end{split} (11)

However, if one consider that the Beddington-DeAngelis like functional response is coming out of an asymptotics when ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 of (8), one should rather study the possible appearance of patterns starting from system (9). We will describe the study that we performed concerning this issue in Subsection 1.3 of the Introduction. Note that for Holling-type II functional response, no patterns appear when the cross diffusion model (6) is considered, at least under the (biologically reasonable) assumption d3<d2d_{3}<d_{2}, so that the qualitative behavior of (3) and (6) is not expected to be different.

1.2 Rigorous results of convergence

We consider in this subsection the system (8) in a smooth bounded open subset Ω\Omega of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}:

∂tNε−d1​Δx​Nε\displaystyle\partial_{t}N^{\varepsilon}-d_{1}\Delta_{x}N^{\varepsilon} =r0​(1−η​Nε)​Nε−α​Nε​psε1+ξ​psε,\displaystyle=r_{0}\left(1-\eta N^{\varepsilon}\right)N^{\varepsilon}-\dfrac{\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}{1+\xi p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}, (12)
∂tpsε−d2​Δx​psε\displaystyle\partial_{t}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}-d_{2}\Delta_{x}p_{s}^{\varepsilon} =1ε​(−α​Nε​psε1+ξ​psε+γ~​phε)+Γ​phε−μ​psε,\displaystyle=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\bigg(-\frac{\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}{1+\xi p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}+\tilde{\gamma}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\bigg)+\Gamma p_{h}^{\varepsilon}-\mu p_{s}^{\varepsilon}, (13)
∂tphε−d3​Δx​phε\displaystyle\partial_{t}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}-d_{3}\Delta_{x}p_{h}^{\varepsilon} =−1ε​(−α​Nε​psε1+ξ​psε+γ~​phε)−μ​phε,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\bigg(-\frac{\alpha N^{\varepsilon}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}{1+\xi p_{s}^{\varepsilon}}+\tilde{\gamma}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\bigg)-\mu p_{h}^{\varepsilon}, (14)

together with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions (n^​(x)\hat{n}(x) denoting the exterior normal to Ω\Omega at a point x∈∂Ωx\in\partial\Omega)

∀x∈∂Ω,n^​(x)⋅∇xNε=0,n^​(x)⋅∇xpsε=0,n^​(x)⋅∇xphε=0.\forall x\in\partial\Omega,\qquad\hat{n}(x)\cdot\nabla_{x}N^{\varepsilon}=0,\quad\hat{n}(x)\cdot\nabla_{x}p_{s}^{\varepsilon}=0,\quad\hat{n}(x)\cdot\nabla_{x}p_{h}^{\varepsilon}=0. (15)

All parameters r0r_{0}, α\alpha, γ~\tilde{\gamma}, Γ\Gamma, μ\mu, did_{i} in this system are strictly positive, except η\eta and ξ\xi, which are supposed to be nonnegative. When η=0\eta=0, no direct logistic saturation is imposed on the preys, while when ξ=0\xi=0, no competition between predators is assumed. Note that when both η\eta and ξ\xi are equal to zero, the reaction part of the system (12)-(14) reduces to (4).

We begin with a rigorous result for the passage to the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 in the case ξ=0\xi=0:

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ω\Omega be a smooth bounded open subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (for some dimension d∈ℕ−{0}d\in\mathbb{N}-\{0\}), d1,d2,d3>0d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}>0 be diffusion rates, r0,α,γ~,Γ,μ>0r_{0},\;\alpha,\;\tilde{\gamma}\;,\Gamma,\;\mu>0 and η≥0\eta\geq 0 be parameters, and Ni​n:=Ni​n​(x)≥0N_{in}:=N_{in}(x)\geq 0, ph,i​n:=ph,i​n​(x)≥0p_{h,in}:=p_{h,in}(x)\geq 0, ps,i​n:=ps,i​n​(x)≥0p_{s,in}:=p_{s,in}(x)\geq 0 be nonnegative initial data respectively in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega), L2+δ​(Ω)L^{2+\delta}(\Omega), and L2+δ​(Ω)L^{2+\delta}(\Omega) for some δ>0\delta>0.

Then for each ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a unique global classical (for t>0t>0) solution (NεN^{\varepsilon}, phεp_{h}^{\varepsilon}, psεp_{s}^{\varepsilon}) to system (12) – (15) with ξ=0\xi=0 (with the initial data defined above).

Moreover, when ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, one can extract from NεN^{\varepsilon} a subsequence which is bounded in L∞​([0,T]×Ω)L^{\infty}([0,T]\times\Omega) for all T>0T>0 and converges a.e. towards a function N≥0N\geq 0 lying in L∞​([0,T]×Ω)L^{\infty}([0,T]\times\Omega). One can also extract from psεp_{s}^{\varepsilon} (resp. phεp_{h}^{\varepsilon}) a subsequence which converges weakly in L2+δ​([0,T]×Ω)L^{2+\delta}([0,T]\times\Omega) towards a function ps≥0p_{s}\geq 0 (resp. ph≥0p_{h}\geq 0) lying in L2+δ​([0,T]×Ω)L^{2+\delta}([0,T]\times\Omega) for all T>0T>0 and some δ>0\delta>0.

Finally, NN, psp_{s} and php_{h} are very-weak solutions of the cross-diffusion system

∂t\displaystyle\partial_{t} N−d1​Δx​N=r0​(1−η​N)​N−α​N​ps,\displaystyle N-d_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r_{0}(1-\eta N)N-\alpha Np_{s}, (16)

α​N​ps=γ~​ph,\displaystyle\alpha Np_{s}=\tilde{\gamma}p_{h}, (18)

∀x∈∂Ω,n^​(x)⋅∇xN=0,n^​(x)⋅∇xps=0,\forall x\in\partial\Omega,\qquad\hat{n}(x)\cdot\nabla_{x}N=0,\quad\hat{n}(x)\cdot\nabla_{x}p_{s}=0, (19)

N⁡(0,x)=Ni​n​(x),(ps+ph)​(0,x)=ps,i​n​(x)+ph,i​n​(x),N(0,x)=N_{in}(x),\qquad(p_{s}+p_{h})(0,x)=p_{s,in}(x)+p_{h,in}(x), (20)

in the following sense: identity (18) holds a.e., and for all φ,ψ∈𝒞c2([0,+∞)×Ω¯)\varphi,\psi\in\mathcal{C}^{2}_{c}([0,+\infty)\times\bar{\Omega}) such that ∇xφ⋅n|∂Ω=0,∇xψ⋅n|∂Ω=0\nabla_{x}\varphi\cdot n_{|_{\partial\Omega}}=0,\;\nabla_{x}\psi\cdot n_{|_{\partial\Omega}}=0,

−∫0∞∫ΩN∂tφ−∫Ωφ(0,⋅)Ni​n−d1∫0∞∫ΩNΔxφ=∫0∞∫Ω(r0(1−ηN)N−αNps)φ,-\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}N\partial_{t}\varphi-\int_{\Omega}\varphi(0,\cdot)N_{in}-d_{1}\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}N\Delta_{x}\varphi=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}(r_{0}(1-\eta N)N-\alpha Np_{s})\varphi, (21)
−∫0∞∫Ω(ps+ph)∂tψ−∫Ωψ(0,⋅)(ps,i​n+ph,i​n)−∫0∞∫Ω(d2ps+d3ph)Δxψ=∫0∞∫Ω(Γph−μ(ph+ps))ψ.-\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}(p_{s}+p_{h})\partial_{t}\psi-\int_{\Omega}\psi(0,\cdot)(p_{s,in}+p_{h,in})-\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}(d_{2}p_{s}+d_{3}p_{h})\Delta_{x}\psi=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}(\Gamma p_{h}-\mu(p_{h}+p_{s}))\psi. (22)

1.3 Study of the Turing instability

In Section 3 of this paper, we study the Turing instability regions associated to systems (9) and (11). In order to do so, we first perform an adimensionalization, which enables to keep only a small number of parameters in the equations. Then we make explicit the condition on the parameters which leads to the existence of an homogeneous coexistence equilibrium for (9) and (11). We also perform a linear stability analysis of this equilibrium (when it exists) at the level of ODEs (that is, w.r.t. homogeneous perturbations), and at the level of PDEs. Thus, we show that the Turing instability region (in terms of parameters) is nonempty, as expected, for both systems (9) and (11). Finally, we compare the size of these regions. The main point is the fact that the Turing instability region associated to system (9) is always strictly included in the Turing instability region of system (11).

As a consequence, the use of reaction-diffusion systems for predator-prey interactions of Beddington-DeAngelis like in which standard diffusion is simply added to the reaction terms may lead to an overestimate of the possibility of appearance of patterns (at least in the case when the Beddington-DeAngelis functional response is a consequence of the interactions of searching and handling predators).

It is worth to mention that in some instances, the introduction of cross-diffusion terms instead of standard (linear) diffusion terms leads exactly to the opposite result, that is, the increase of the set of parameter values in which patterns develop, or even the appearance of patterns when none were observed with a linear diffusion [32, 33].

∂N∂t−d1​Δx​N=r0​(1−Nk)​N−γ~​2​α​N​PB+Δ,∂P∂t−Δx​(d2​2​γ~​PA+Δ+d3​2​α​N​PB+Δ)=Γ​2​α​N​PB+Δ−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dfrac{\partial N}{\partial t}&-d_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r_{0}\left(1-\dfrac{N}{k}\right)N-\tilde{\gamma}\dfrac{2\alpha NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}},\\[8.5359pt] \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial t}&-\Delta_{x}\left(d_{2}\dfrac{2\tilde{\gamma}P}{A+\sqrt{\Delta}}+d_{3}\dfrac{2\alpha NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}\right)=\Gamma\dfrac{2\alpha NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}-\mu P,\end{split} (68)

where A,BA,\;B and Δ\Delta are defined in (66) and (67).

3.2 Adimensionalization

In order to simplify the notations and to keep only meaningful parameters, we now propose an adimensionalization procedure, using the new variables T,n,pT,\;n,\;p instead of t,N,Pt,\;N,\;P in the following way:

t=Θ​T,N=Σ​n,P=Π​p.t=\Theta T,\;N=\Sigma n,\;P=\Pi p.

After simplifications, the system (68) becomes

∂n∂T\displaystyle\dfrac{\partial n}{\partial T} −d1​Θ​Δx​n=r0​Θ​(1−nk/Σ)​n−2​γ~​α​Π​Θ​n​pB+Δ,\displaystyle-d_{1}\Theta\Delta_{x}n=r_{0}\Theta\left(1-\dfrac{n}{k/\Sigma}\right)n-\dfrac{2\tilde{\gamma}\alpha\Pi\Theta np}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}},
∂p∂T\displaystyle\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial T} −Δx​(d2​Θ​2​γ~​pA+Δ+d3​Θ​2​α​Σ​n​pB+Δ)=2​Γ​α​Σ​Θ​n​pB+Δ−μ​Θ​p,\displaystyle-\Delta_{x}\left(d_{2}\Theta\dfrac{2\tilde{\gamma}p}{A+\sqrt{\Delta}}+d_{3}\Theta\dfrac{2\alpha\Sigma np}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}\right)=\dfrac{2\Gamma\alpha\Sigma\Theta np}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}-\mu\Theta p,

where

A+Δ\displaystyle A+\sqrt{\Delta} =γ~+α​Σ​n−γ~​ξ​Π​p+(γ~+α​Σ​n+γ~​ξ​Π​p)2−4​γ~​α​ξ​Σ​Π​n​p,\displaystyle=\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha\Sigma n-\tilde{\gamma}\xi\Pi p+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha\Sigma n+\tilde{\gamma}\xi\Pi p)^{2}-4\tilde{\gamma}\alpha\xi\Sigma\Pi np},
B+Δ\displaystyle B+\sqrt{\Delta} =γ~+α​Σ​n+γ~​ξ​Π​p+(γ~+α​Σ​n+γ~​ξ​Π​p)2−4​γ~​α​ξ​Σ​Π​n​p.\displaystyle=\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha\Sigma n+\tilde{\gamma}\xi\Pi p+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+\alpha\Sigma n+\tilde{\gamma}\xi\Pi p)^{2}-4\tilde{\gamma}\alpha\xi\Sigma\Pi np}.

Choosing Θ,Σ,Π\Theta,\;\Sigma,\;\Pi in such a way that 2​α​Π​Θ=1,α​Σ=1,γ~​ξ​Π=12\alpha\Pi\Theta=1,\;\alpha\Sigma=1,\;\tilde{\gamma}\xi\Pi=1, we end up with the system

∂n∂T−d1​Θ​Δx​n=r0​Θ​(1−nk/Σ)​n−γ~​n​pB+Δ,\displaystyle\dfrac{\partial n}{\partial T}-d_{1}\Theta\Delta_{x}n=r_{0}\Theta\left(1-\dfrac{n}{k/\Sigma}\right)n-\dfrac{\tilde{\gamma}np}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}},
∂p∂T−Δx​(d2​Θ​2​γ~​pA+Δ+d3​Θ​2​n​pB+Δ)=Γ​γ~​Σ​ξ​n​pB+Δ−μ​Θ​p,\displaystyle\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial T}-\Delta_{x}\left(d_{2}\Theta\dfrac{2\tilde{\gamma}p}{A+\sqrt{\Delta}}+d_{3}\Theta\dfrac{2np}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}\right)=\dfrac{\Gamma\tilde{\gamma}\Sigma\xi np}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}-\mu\Theta p,

where now

A+Δ\displaystyle A+\sqrt{\Delta} =γ~+n−p+(γ~+n+p)2−4​n​p,\displaystyle=\tilde{\gamma}+n-p+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+n+p)^{2}-4np},
B+Δ\displaystyle B+\sqrt{\Delta} =γ~+n+p+(γ~+n+p)2−4​n​p.\displaystyle=\tilde{\gamma}+n+p+\sqrt{(\tilde{\gamma}+n+p)^{2}-4np}.

We set D1:=d1​Θ,D2:=d2​Θ,D3:=d3​Θ,r=r0​Θ,ν:=k/ΣD_{1}:=d_{1}\Theta,\;D_{2}:=d_{2}\Theta,\;D_{3}:=d_{3}\Theta,\;r=r_{0}\Theta,\;\nu:=k/\Sigma.
Furthermore, we denote again nn by NN, pp by PP, γ~\tilde{\gamma} by γ\gamma, and redefine Γ:=Γ​γ~​Σ​ξ,μ:=μ​Θ\Gamma:=\Gamma\tilde{\gamma}\Sigma\xi,\;\mu:=\mu\Theta. We end up with

∂N∂T−D1​Δx​N=r⁡(1−Nν)​N−γ​N​PB+Δ,∂P∂T−Δx​(D2​2​γ​PA+Δ+D3​2​N​PB+Δ)=Γ​N​PB+Δ−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dfrac{\partial N}{\partial T}&-D_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r\left(1-\dfrac{N}{\nu}\right)N-\dfrac{\gamma NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}},\\[8.5359pt] \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial T}&-\Delta_{x}\left(D_{2}\dfrac{2\gamma P}{A+\sqrt{\Delta}}+D_{3}\dfrac{2NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}\right)=\dfrac{\Gamma NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}-\mu P,\end{split} (69)

where now

A=γ+N−P,B=γ+N+P,Δ=(γ+N+P)2−4​N​P.A=\gamma+N-P,\quad B=\gamma+N+P,\quad\Delta=(\gamma+N+P)^{2}-4NP. (70)

Rationalizing the denominators, we can obtain an equivalent expression, which is useful for the stability analysis of equilibrium states:

∂N∂T−D1​Δx​N=r⁡(1−Nν)​N−γ4​(B−B2−4​N​P),∂P∂T−Δx​(D22​(Δ−A)+D32​(B−Δ))=Γ4​(B−B2−4​N​P)−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dfrac{\partial N}{\partial T}&-D_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r\left(1-\dfrac{N}{\nu}\right)N-\dfrac{\gamma}{4}\left(B-\sqrt{B^{2}-4NP}\right),\\[8.5359pt] \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial T}&-\Delta_{x}\left(\dfrac{D_{2}}{2}{(\sqrt{\Delta}-A)}+\dfrac{D_{3}}{2}{(B-\sqrt{\Delta})}\right)=\dfrac{\Gamma}{4}\left(B-\sqrt{B^{2}-4NP}\right)-\mu P,\end{split} (71)

where A,BA,\;B and Δ\Delta are still defined by (70).

The limiting system presents a cross-diffusion term in the predator equation (the diffusion rate depends on the prey biomass), and a trophic function close to the Beddington-DeAngelis one.

3.3 Homogeneous equilibrium states

In this subsection, we look for the equilibrium states of the ODEs system corresponding to the reaction part of the whole system (69), or equivalently (71):

N˙=r⁡(1−Nν)​N−γ​N​PB+Δ,P˙=Γ​N​PB+Δ−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dot{N}&=r\left(1-\dfrac{N}{\nu}\right)N-\dfrac{\gamma NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}},\\[14.22636pt] \dot{P}&=\dfrac{\Gamma NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}-\mu P,\end{split} (72)

where A,BA,\;B and Δ\Delta are defined in (70).

From the first equation, if P=0P=0 we obtain N=0N=0 or N=νN=\nu, corresponding to the total extinction E0​(0,0)E_{0}(0,0) and the non-coexistence E1​(ν,0)E_{1}(\nu,0) equilibria.

Otherwise, we look for a coexistence equilibrium E∗​(N∗,P∗)E_{*}(N_{*},P_{*}) (that means N∗,P∗>0N_{*},\;P_{*}>0). From the second equation, we get the identity

Γ​N∗γ+N∗+P∗+(γ+N∗+P∗)2−4​N∗​P∗−μ=0,\dfrac{\Gamma N_{*}}{\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*}+\sqrt{(\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*})^{2}-4N_{*}P_{*}}}-\mu=0, (73)

from which, rationalizing the denominator, we can obtain

(γ+N∗+P∗)2−4​N∗​P∗=γ+N∗+P∗−4​μΓ​P∗.\sqrt{(\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*})^{2}-4N_{*}P_{*}}=\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*}-\dfrac{4\mu}{\Gamma}P_{*}. (74)

Rewriting (73) as

Γ​N∗−μ⁡(γ+N∗+P∗)=μ​(γ+N∗+P∗)2−4​N∗​P∗,\Gamma N_{*}-\mu(\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*})=\mu\sqrt{(\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*})^{2}-4N_{*}P_{*}},

we see that the searched equilibrium can exist only if

Γ​N∗−μ⁡(γ+N∗+P∗)>0.\Gamma N_{*}-\mu(\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*})>0. (75)

Taking the square of both terms, we end up with

P∗=Γ2​μ​(Γ−2​μ)​N∗−2​γ​μ(Γ−2​μ)=Γ2​μ​N∗−Γ​γΓ−2​μ.P_{*}=\dfrac{\Gamma}{2\mu}\dfrac{(\Gamma-2\mu)N_{*}-2\gamma\mu}{(\Gamma-2\mu)}=\dfrac{\Gamma}{2\mu}N_{*}-\dfrac{\Gamma\gamma}{\Gamma-2\mu}. (76)

Substituting (76) in (75), we see that (75) is equivalent to

Γ−2​μ2​N∗+γ​μ​(2​μΓ−2​μ)>0.\dfrac{\Gamma-2\mu}{2}N_{*}+\gamma\mu\left(\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma-2\mu}\right)>0. (77)

Since we are looking for equilibria with N∗>0N_{*}>0. we see that (75) or (77) can also be rewritten as

Γ−2​μ>0.\Gamma-2\mu>0. (78)

Substituting the expression (74) in the equation N˙=0\dot{N}=0 from the first equation of (72) written as

N˙=r⁡(1−Nν)​N−γ4​(B−Δ),\dot{N}=r\left(1-\dfrac{N}{\nu}\right)N-\dfrac{\gamma}{4}{(B-\sqrt{\Delta})},

we obtain

r⁡(1−Nν)​N−γ​μΓ​P∗=0,r\left(1-\dfrac{N}{\nu}\right)N-\dfrac{\gamma\mu}{\Gamma}P_{*}=0, (79)

from which we have another expression of P∗P_{*} in terms of N∗N_{*}:

P∗=Γγ​μ​r​(1−N∗ν)​N∗.P_{*}=\dfrac{\Gamma}{\gamma\mu}r\left(1-\dfrac{N_{*}}{\nu}\right)N_{*}. (80)

Substituting the expression (76) in (79), we obtain a second order equation in the unknown N∗N_{*}:

rν​N∗2−(r−γ2)​N∗−μ​γ2Γ−2​μ=0.\dfrac{r}{\nu}N_{*}^{2}-\left(r-\dfrac{\gamma}{2}\right)N_{*}-\dfrac{\mu\gamma^{2}}{\Gamma-2\mu}=0. (81)

We see that, thanks to (78),

ΔN:=(r−γ2)2+4​rν​μ​γ2Γ−2​μ>0,\Delta_{N}:=\left(r-\dfrac{\gamma}{2}\right)^{2}+4\dfrac{r}{\nu}\dfrac{\mu\gamma^{2}}{\Gamma-2\mu}>0, (82)

so that equation (81) has one and only one strictly positive solution, given by

N∗=ν2​r​(r−γ2+ΔN).N_{*}=\dfrac{\nu}{2r}\left(r-\dfrac{\gamma}{2}+\sqrt{\Delta_{N}}\right). (83)

Then, the condition P∗>0P_{*}>0 is equivalent to

Γ2​μ​N∗−Γ​γΓ−2​μ>0⇔ 0<N∗<ν,\dfrac{\Gamma}{2\mu}N_{*}-\dfrac{\Gamma\gamma}{\Gamma-2\mu}>0\;\Leftrightarrow\;0<N_{*}<\nu, (84)

depending on the chosen expression for P∗P_{*}. This condition can be rewritten as

Γ−2​μ>2​γ​μν,\Gamma-2\mu>\dfrac{2\gamma\mu}{\nu}, (85)

by substituting (83) in the last term of (84). Note that this last necessary condition for the existence of the coexistence equilibrium E∗E_{*} implies condition (78). We now briefly explain why condition (85) is in fact both necessary and sufficient for the existence of E∗E_{*}. Indeed, (85) can be rewritten as

ΔN<r+γ2,\sqrt{\Delta_{N}}<r+\dfrac{\gamma}{2},

so that N∗N_{*} (computed from formula (83) and (82)) is such that 0<N∗<ν0<N_{*}<\nu. Remembering that this last condition is equivalent to P∗>0P_{*}>0 (when P∗P_{*} is given by (80) for example), we see that both N∗N_{*} and P∗P_{*} defined in this way are strictly positive. One can easily check that they satisfy N˙=0,P˙=0\dot{N}=0,\;\dot{P}=0 in (72).

We now study the stability properties of these equilibrium states. We denote as Ji​j,i,j=1,2J_{ij},\;i,j=1,2, the elements of the Jacobian matrix of the system (72):

J11\displaystyle J_{11} =∂∂N​N˙=r−2​rν​N−γ4​(1−γ+N−P(γ+N+P)2−4​N​P),\displaystyle=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial N}\dot{N}=r-\dfrac{2r}{\nu}N-\dfrac{\gamma}{4}\left(1-\dfrac{\gamma+N-P}{\sqrt{(\gamma+N+P)^{2}-4NP}}\right),

J21\displaystyle J_{21} =∂∂N​P˙=Γ4​(1−γ+N−P(γ+N+P)2−4​N​P),\displaystyle=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial N}\dot{P}=\dfrac{\Gamma}{4}\left(1-\dfrac{\gamma+N-P}{\sqrt{(\gamma+N+P)^{2}-4NP}}\right),

Evaluating the Jacobian matrix in the equilibrium states, we obtain:

J⁡(E0)=[r00−μ],J⁡(E1)=[−r∗0J22​(E1)]J(E_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}r&0\\ 0&-\mu\end{bmatrix},\qquad J(E_{1})=\begin{bmatrix}-r&*\\ 0&J_{22}(E_{1})\end{bmatrix}

(where ∗* in the matrix means “some term that we do not make explicit”), and

J22(E1)=Γ​ν2​(γ+ν)−μ>0⇔Γ−2μ>2​γ​μν.J_{22}(E_{1})=\dfrac{\Gamma\nu}{2(\gamma+\nu)}-\mu>0\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad\Gamma-2\mu>\dfrac{2\gamma\mu}{\nu}.

Then the equilibrium E0E_{0} is unstable (it is a saddle point); the equilibrium E1E_{1} is locally asymptotically stable (it is a node) when E∗E_{*} does not exist, and unstable (it is a saddle point) otherwise.

The study of the stability of E∗E_{*} is more intricate. First, we compute the quantities

Q∗:=γ+N∗+P∗−4​μΓ​P∗=Γ−2​μ2​μ​N∗+2​μ​γΓ−2​μ>0Q_{*}:=\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*}-\dfrac{4\mu}{\Gamma}P_{*}=\dfrac{\Gamma-2\mu}{2\mu}N_{*}+\dfrac{2\mu\gamma}{\Gamma-2\mu}>0 (86)

and, thank to (76) and (86),

P∗Q∗=ΓΓ−2​μ​(1−2​μ​γ​Γ(Γ−2​μ)2​N∗+4​μ2​γ).\dfrac{P_{*}}{Q_{*}}=\dfrac{\Gamma}{\Gamma-2\mu}\left(1-\dfrac{2\mu\gamma\Gamma}{(\Gamma-2\mu)^{2}N_{*}+4\mu^{2}\gamma}\right).

=−rQ∗​2​μ​γΓ−2​μ​[(Γ−2​μ)24​ν​μ2​γ​N∗2+2ν​N∗−1]\displaystyle=-\dfrac{r}{Q_{*}}\dfrac{2\mu\gamma}{\Gamma-2\mu}\left[\dfrac{(\Gamma-2\mu)^{2}}{4\nu\mu^{2}\gamma}N_{*}^{2}+\dfrac{2}{\nu}N_{*}-1\right]
=μ​γ2​Γ(Γ−2​μ)2​N∗+4​μ2​γ−ΔN,\displaystyle=\dfrac{\mu\gamma^{2}\Gamma}{(\Gamma-2\mu)^{2}N_{*}+4\mu^{2}\gamma}-\sqrt{\Delta_{N}},
J12∗:=J12​(E∗)\displaystyle J^{*}_{12}:=J_{12}(E_{*}) =−γ4​((γ+N∗+P∗)2−4​N∗​P∗−(γ+N∗+P∗)+2​N∗(γ+N∗+P∗)2−4​N∗​P∗)\displaystyle=-\dfrac{\gamma}{4}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{(\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*})^{2}-4N_{*}P_{*}}-(\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*})+2N_{*}}{\sqrt{(\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*})^{2}-4N_{*}P_{*}}}\right)

det𝑱∗=rQ∗2​(1−N∗ν)​N∗​[r⁡((Γ−2​μ)22​ν​μ​γ​N∗2+4​μν​N∗−2​μ)+Γ​γ2],\det\bm{J}^{*}=\dfrac{r}{Q_{*}^{2}}\left(1-\dfrac{N_{*}}{\nu}\right)N_{*}\left[r\left(\dfrac{(\Gamma-2\mu)^{2}}{2\nu\mu\gamma}N_{*}^{2}+\dfrac{4\mu}{\nu}N_{*}-2\mu\right)+\dfrac{\Gamma\gamma}{2}\right],

On the contrary, the sign of the trace of the Jacobin matrix evaluated at E∗E_{*} is not prescribed. Indeed, when J11∗<0J^{*}_{11}<0, we have

and then E∗E_{*} is locally asymptotically stable. However, when J11∗>0J^{*}_{11}>0, the trace can be nonpositive or nonnegative. Numerical evidences show that both cases can hold for different values of the parameters of the model.

3.4 Turing Instability when linear diffusions are added to the system of ODEs

We consider the system of reaction-diffusion defined by (for given D1,DP>0D_{1},D_{P}>0)

∂N∂t−D1​Δx​N=r⁡(1−Nν)​N−γ​N​PB+Δ,∂P∂t−DP​Δx​P=Γ​N​PB+Δ−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dfrac{\partial N}{\partial t}&-D_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r\left(1-\dfrac{N}{\nu}\right)N-\dfrac{\gamma NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}},\\[8.5359pt] \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial t}&-D_{P}\Delta_{x}P=\dfrac{\Gamma NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}-\mu P,\end{split} (87)

where A,BA,\;B and Δ\Delta are defined in (70), and sets of parameter values such that tr ​J​(E∗)<0\textnormal{tr }J(E_{*})<0 (Note that such parameters indeed exist).
For any λk≥0\lambda_{k}\geq 0 eigenvalue of the Laplacian on Ω\Omega (with Neumann boundary conditions), where k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the characteristic matrix evaluated at the equilibrium E∗E_{*}

𝑴=[J11∗−D1​λkJ12∗J21∗J22∗−DP​λk]\bm{M}=\begin{bmatrix}J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{12}\\ J^{*}_{21}&J^{*}_{22}-D_{P}\lambda_{k}\end{bmatrix}

has a strictly negative trace. In fact,

T​r​𝑴=J11∗−D1​λk+J22∗−DP​λk=tr ​𝑱−D1​λk−D2​λk<0.Tr\bm{M}=J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}+J^{*}_{22}-D_{P}\lambda_{k}=\textnormal{tr }\bm{J}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}-D_{2}\lambda_{k}<0.

Its determinant is

det𝑴=det𝑱−(DP​J11∗+D1​J22∗)​λk+D1​DP​λk2,\det\bm{M}=\det\bm{J}-(D_{P}J^{*}_{11}+D_{1}J^{*}_{22})\lambda_{k}+D_{1}D_{P}\lambda_{k}^{2},

so that a necessary condition for the Turing instability to appear is

D1​J22∗+DP​J11∗>0.D_{1}J^{*}_{22}+D_{P}J^{*}_{11}>0.

If J11∗<0J^{*}_{11}<0, remembering that J22∗<0J_{22}^{*}<0, we see that DP​J11∗+D1​J22∗<0D_{P}J^{*}_{11}+D_{1}J^{*}_{22}<0, so that no Turing instability can appear.

On the opposite, if J11∗>0J^{*}_{11}>0, for any given k≠0k\neq 0 (so that λk>0\lambda_{k}>0), we can select DPD_{P} sufficiently large for getting det𝑱−DP​J11∗​λk<0\det\bm{J}-D_{P}J^{*}_{11}\lambda_{k}<0. Then, when D1>0D_{1}>0 is small enough, det𝑴<0\det\bm{M}<0 and the Turing instability appears.

3.5 Turing Instability with cross diffusion

We now consider system (69) or the equivalent form (71), that is

∂N∂T−D1​Δx​N=r⁡(1−Nν)​N−γ4​(B−B2−4​N​P),∂P∂T−Δx​(D22​(Δ−A)+D32​(B−Δ))=Γ4​(B−B2−4​N​P)−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dfrac{\partial N}{\partial T}&-D_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r\left(1-\dfrac{N}{\nu}\right)N-\dfrac{\gamma}{4}\left(B-\sqrt{B^{2}-4NP}\right),\\[8.5359pt] \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial T}&-\Delta_{x}\left(\dfrac{D_{2}}{2}{(\sqrt{\Delta}-A)}+\dfrac{D_{3}}{2}{(B-\sqrt{\Delta})}\right)=\dfrac{\Gamma}{4}\left(B-\sqrt{B^{2}-4NP}\right)-\mu P,\end{split}

where A,BA,\;B and Δ\Delta are defined by (70). The characteristic matrix takes the form

𝑴:=[J11∗−JΔ​11∗​λkJ12∗−JΔ​12∗​λkJ21∗−JΔ​21∗​λkJ22∗−JΔ​22∗​λk],\bm{M}:=\begin{bmatrix}J^{*}_{11}-J^{*}_{\Delta 11}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{12}-J^{*}_{\Delta 12}\lambda_{k}\\[5.69046pt] J^{*}_{21}-J^{*}_{\Delta 21}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{22}-J^{*}_{\Delta 22}\lambda_{k}\end{bmatrix},

where the λk\lambda_{k} are defined as in Subsection 3.4, and the terms JΔ​i​j,i,j=1,2J_{\Delta ij},\;i,j=1,2 are obtained by linearizing the diffusion terms around E∗E_{*}. Their explicit form is given by the following formulas:

JΔ​11∗\displaystyle J^{*}_{\Delta 11} =D1>0,\displaystyle=D_{1}>0,
JΔ​12∗\displaystyle J^{*}_{\Delta 12} =0,\displaystyle=0,
JΔ​21∗\displaystyle J^{*}_{\Delta 21} =D2−D32​((γ+N∗−P∗)−Δ∗Δ∗)=−D2−D3Q∗​Γ−2​μΓ​P∗,\displaystyle=\dfrac{D_{2}-D_{3}}{2}\left(\dfrac{(\gamma+N_{*}-P_{*})-\sqrt{\Delta_{*}}}{\sqrt{\Delta_{*}}}\right)=-\dfrac{D_{2}-D_{3}}{Q_{*}}\dfrac{\Gamma-2\mu}{\Gamma}P_{*}, (88)
JΔ​22∗\displaystyle J^{*}_{\Delta 22} =D22​((γ−N∗+P∗)+Δ∗Δ∗)+D32​(Δ∗−(γ−N∗+P∗)Δ∗)\displaystyle=\dfrac{D_{2}}{2}\left(\dfrac{(\gamma-N_{*}+P_{*})+\sqrt{\Delta_{*}}}{\sqrt{\Delta_{*}}}\right)+\dfrac{D_{3}}{2}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{\Delta_{*}}-(\gamma-N_{*}+P_{*})}{\sqrt{\Delta_{*}}}\right)
=D2Q∗​(γ+P∗​(Γ−2​μ)Γ)+D3Q∗​2​μ​γΓ−2​μ>0.\displaystyle=\dfrac{D_{2}}{Q_{*}}\left(\gamma+P_{*}\dfrac{(\Gamma-2\mu)}{\Gamma}\right)+\dfrac{D_{3}}{Q_{*}}\dfrac{2\mu\gamma}{\Gamma-2\mu}>0. (89)

We notice that only the sign of JΔ​212J^{2}_{\Delta 21} depends on D2,D3D_{2},D_{3}. Due to the biological meaning of these parameters, we systematically assume that D2>D3D_{2}>D_{3}. Indeed, searching predators are expected to diffuse more quickly than handling predators. With this assumption, JΔ​21∗<0J^{*}_{\Delta 21}<0.

We still consider sets of parameter values such that tr ​J​(E∗)<0\textnormal{tr }J(E_{*})<0. Then the characteristic matrix 𝑴\bm{M} has strictly negative trace, because

tr ​𝑴=J11∗−D1​λk+J22∗−JΔ​22∗​λk=tr ​𝑱∗⏟−−D1​λk−JΔ​22∗⏟+​λk<0.\textnormal{tr }\bm{M}=J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}+J^{*}_{22}-J^{*}_{\Delta 22}\lambda_{k}=\underbrace{\textnormal{tr }\bm{J}^{*}}_{-}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}-\underbrace{J^{*}_{\Delta 22}}_{+}\lambda_{k}<0.

Its determinant is

det𝑴=det𝑱∗⏟+−(J11∗​JΔ​22∗+J22∗​JΔ​11∗−J12∗​JΔ​21∗)​λk+(D1​JΔ​22∗)⏟+​λk2,\det\bm{M}=\underbrace{\det\bm{J}^{*}}_{+}-(J^{*}_{11}J^{*}_{\Delta 22}+J^{*}_{22}J^{*}_{\Delta 11}-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{\Delta 21})\lambda_{k}+\underbrace{(D_{1}J^{*}_{\Delta 22})}_{+}\lambda_{k}^{2},

so that a necessary condition for the Turing instability to appear is

J11∗​JΔ​22∗+J22∗​JΔ​11∗−J12∗​JΔ​21∗>0.J^{*}_{11}J^{*}_{\Delta 22}+J^{*}_{22}J^{*}_{\Delta 11}-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{\Delta 21}>0. (90)

If J11∗<0J^{*}_{11}<0, we have

J11∗⏟−​JΔ​22∗⏟++J22∗⏟−​JΔ​11∗⏟+−J12∗⏟−​JΔ​21∗⏟−,\underbrace{J^{*}_{11}}_{-}\underbrace{J^{*}_{\Delta 22}}_{+}+\underbrace{J^{*}_{22}}_{-}\underbrace{J^{*}_{\Delta 11}}_{+}-\underbrace{J^{*}_{12}}_{-}\underbrace{J^{*}_{\Delta 21}}_{-},

so that condition (90) does not hold and, as in the case of linear diffusion, no Turing instability can appear. On the opposite, if J11∗>0J^{*}_{11}>0, we have

J11∗⏟+​JΔ​22∗⏟++J22∗⏟−​JΔ​11∗⏟+−J12∗⏟−​JΔ​21∗⏟−.\underbrace{J^{*}_{11}}_{+}\underbrace{J^{*}_{\Delta 22}}_{+}+\underbrace{J^{*}_{22}}_{-}\underbrace{J^{*}_{\Delta 11}}_{+}-\underbrace{J^{*}_{12}}_{-}\underbrace{J^{*}_{\Delta 21}}_{-}.

Then, for any k≠0k\neq 0 (so that λk>0\lambda_{k}>0, we can select D2D_{2} large enough and D3∼D2D_{3}\sim D_{2} so that det𝑱−(J11∗​JΔ​22∗−J12∗​JΔ​21∗)​λk<0\det\bm{J}-(J^{*}_{11}J^{*}_{\Delta 22}-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{\Delta 21})\lambda_{k}<0. Then, when D1>0D_{1}>0 is small enough, det𝑴<0\det\bm{M}<0 and the Turing instability appears.

3.6 Turing instability regions: linear versus cross diffusion

We recall that the derivation of equations (69) produces a cross diffusion term in the predator equation, whereas the prey diffusion rate is still a constant. We recall, for reader’s convenience, the model equations

∂N∂T−D1​Δx​N=r⁡(1−Nν)​N−γ​N​PB+Δ,∂P∂T−Δx​(f⁡(P,N)​P)=Γ​N​PB+Δ−μ​P,\displaystyle\begin{split}\dfrac{\partial N}{\partial T}&-D_{1}\Delta_{x}N=r\left(1-\dfrac{N}{\nu}\right)N-\dfrac{\gamma NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}},\\[8.5359pt] \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial T}&-\Delta_{x}\left(f(P,N)P\right)=\dfrac{\Gamma NP}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}-\mu P,\end{split} (91)

where

A=γ+N−P,B=γ+N+P,Δ=(γ+N+P)2−4​N​P.A=\gamma+N-P,\quad B=\gamma+N+P,\quad\Delta=(\gamma+N+P)^{2}-4NP.

The term Δx​(f​(P,N)​P)\Delta_{x}\left(f(P,N)P\right) is the cross diffusion term, and

f⁡(P,N):=D2​2​γA+Δ+D3​2​NB+Δ.f(P,N):=D_{2}\dfrac{2\gamma}{A+\sqrt{\Delta}}+D_{3}\dfrac{2N}{B+\sqrt{\Delta}}. (92)

We want to compare three natural strategies to model the diffusion in the predator-prey interactions.

  1. 1.

    First, we take the reaction part of (91) and we add a diffusion term with D2D_{2} as constant rate for predators. This means that we exactly take the diffusion coefficient of searching predators for all predators appearing in the limiting model.

  2. 2.

    Secondly, we take the reaction part of (91) and we add a diffusion term with DP=f⁡(P∗,N∗)D_{P}=f(P_{*},N_{*}), where ff is defined in (92), as constant rate of diffusion in the equation for predators. This means that we now take into account the difference among searching and handling predators, since both diffusion rates D2D_{2} and D3D_{3} are present in equation (92).

  3. 3.

    Finally, we consider the cross diffusion model (91), coming out of the derivation of the model by singular perturbation as explained in Section 2 and Subsection 3.1.

Note first that, thanks to (76), it is possible to obtain a simple expression for DPD_{P}. Indeed,

DP\displaystyle D_{P} =f⁡(P∗,N∗)=D2​2​γA∗+Δ∗+D3​2​N∗B∗+Δ∗\displaystyle=f(P_{*},N_{*})=D_{2}\dfrac{2\gamma}{A_{*}+\sqrt{\Delta_{*}}}+D_{3}\dfrac{2N_{*}}{B_{*}+\sqrt{\Delta_{*}}}
=D2​γγ+N∗−2​μΓ​P∗+D3​N∗γ+N∗+P∗−2​μΓ​P∗\displaystyle=D_{2}\dfrac{\gamma}{\gamma+N_{*}-\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}P_{*}}+D_{3}\dfrac{N_{*}}{\gamma+N_{*}+P_{*}-\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}P_{*}}
=D2​γγ+2​μ​γΓ−2​μ+D3​N∗γ+Γ2​μ​N∗−Γ​γΓ−2​μ+2​μ​γΓ−2​μ\displaystyle=D_{2}\dfrac{\gamma}{\gamma+\dfrac{2\mu\gamma}{\Gamma-2\mu}}+D_{3}\dfrac{N_{*}}{\gamma+\dfrac{\Gamma}{2\mu}N_{*}-\dfrac{\Gamma\gamma}{\Gamma-2\mu}+\dfrac{2\mu\gamma}{\Gamma-2\mu}}
=D2​(1−2​μΓ)+D3​2​μΓ.\displaystyle=D_{2}\left(1-\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}\right)+D_{3}\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}. (93)

We notice therefore that DPD_{P} is a convex combination of the diffusion coefficients D2,D3D_{2},\;D_{3} of searching and handling predators. Furthermore, assuming that D3<D2D_{3}<D_{2} (remember that from the modeling point of view, handling predators have a lower diffusion rate than searching predators), we get the estimate

DP=D2​(1−2​μΓ)+D3​2​μΓ=D2−D2−D3Γ​2​μ<D2.D_{P}=D_{2}\left(1-\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}\right)+D_{3}\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}=D_{2}-\dfrac{D_{2}-D_{3}}{\Gamma}2\mu<D_{2}.

The characteristic matrices of the cases that we consider are finally given by

  1. 1.

    Linear diffusion with rate D2D_{2}:

    𝑴L​2=[J11∗−D1​λkJ12∗J21∗J22∗−D2​λk];\bm{M}_{L2}=\begin{bmatrix}J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{12}\\[5.69046pt] J^{*}_{21}&J^{*}_{22}-D_{2}\lambda_{k}\end{bmatrix}; (94)
  2. 2.

    Linear diffusion with rate DPD_{P} defined in (93):

    𝑴L​P=[J11∗−D1​λkJ12∗J21∗J22∗−DP​λk];\bm{M}_{LP}=\begin{bmatrix}J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{12}\\[5.69046pt] J^{*}_{21}&J^{*}_{22}-D_{P}\lambda_{k}\end{bmatrix}; (95)
  3. 3.

    Cross diffusion:

    𝑴C=[J11∗−D1​λkJ12∗J21∗−JΔ​21∗​λkJ22∗−JΔ​22∗​λk];\bm{M}_{C}=\begin{bmatrix}J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{12}\\[5.69046pt] J^{*}_{21}-J^{*}_{\Delta 21}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{22}-J^{*}_{\Delta 22}\lambda_{k}\end{bmatrix}; (96)

    with JΔ​21∗,JΔ​22∗J^{*}_{\Delta 21},\;J^{*}_{\Delta 22} defined in (88) and (89).

We first want to compare the Turing instability regions of the cases 1 and 2, namely the range of the parameters that lead to det𝑴<0\det\bm{M}<0. The characteristic matrices are (94) and (95) where one should remember that D2>DPD_{2}>D_{P} (because of the modeling assumption). Considering the generic matrix of a (linear) diffusion depending on the parameter D>0D>0, we define

𝑴⁡(D):=[J11∗−D1​λkJ12∗J21∗J22∗−D​λk].\bm{M}(D):=\begin{bmatrix}J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{12}\\ J^{*}_{21}&J^{*}_{22}-D\lambda_{k}\end{bmatrix}.

We compute

det𝑴⁡(D)\displaystyle\det\bm{M}(D) =(J11∗−D1​λk)​(J22∗−D​λk)−J12∗​J21∗\displaystyle=\left(J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}\right)\left(J^{*}_{22}-D\lambda_{k}\right)-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21}
=D​D1​λk2−(D1​J22∗+D​J11∗)​λk+det𝑱.\displaystyle=DD_{1}\lambda_{k}^{2}-\left(D_{1}J^{*}_{22}+DJ^{*}_{11}\right)\lambda_{k}+\det\bm{J}.

The interesting case (Turing instability appearance) is obtained under the necessary condition D1​J22∗+D​J11∗>0D_{1}J^{*}_{22}+DJ^{*}_{11}>0, that is

D>D^:=−D1​J22∗J11∗.D>\hat{D}:=-\dfrac{D_{1}J^{*}_{22}}{J^{*}_{11}}.

s​o​l1,2:=(D1​J22∗+D​J11∗)±(D1​J22∗+D​J11∗)2−4​D1​D​(J11∗​J22∗−J12∗​J21∗)2​D1​D.sol_{1,2}:=\dfrac{\left(D_{1}J^{*}_{22}+DJ^{*}_{11}\right)\pm\sqrt{\left(D_{1}J^{*}_{22}+DJ^{*}_{11}\right)^{2}-4D_{1}D(J^{*}_{11}J^{*}_{22}-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21})}}{2D_{1}D}. (97)

(D1(J11∗J22∗−2J12∗J21∗))2−(D1J11∗J22∗)2=−4D12J12∗J21∗detJE∗≥0.(D_{1}(J^{*}_{11}J^{*}_{22}-2J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21}))^{2}-(D_{1}J^{*}_{11}J^{*}_{22})^{2}=-4D_{1}^{2}J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21}\det{J_{E_{*}}}\geq 0.

Then the equation admits two real roots

D^1,2\displaystyle\hat{D}_{1,2} =D1​(J11∗​J22∗−2​J12∗​J21∗)±2​D1​−J∗12J∗21detJE∗J11∗2\displaystyle=\dfrac{D_{1}(J^{*}_{11}J^{*}_{22}-2J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21})\pm 2D_{1}\sqrt{-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21}\det{J_{E_{*}}}}}{J^{*2}_{11}}

which are both nonnegative.

It is also possible to prove that D^1<D^<D^2\hat{D}_{1}<\hat{D}<\hat{D}_{2}. In fact, it can easily be seen that D^2>D^\hat{D}_{2}>\hat{D} is equivalent to

−J∗12J∗21det𝑱∗>−det𝑱∗,\sqrt{-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21}\det\bm{J}^{*}}>-\det\bm{J}^{*},

while D^1<D^\hat{D}_{1}<\hat{D} is equivalent to

−J∗12J∗21det𝑱∗>det𝑱∗,\sqrt{-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21}\det\bm{J}^{*}}>\det\bm{J}^{*},

and can be reduced to J21∗​J22∗<0J^{*}_{21}J^{*}_{22}<0. These conditions are therefore always satisfied. Then the values of DD which lead to Turing Instability are D>D^2D>\hat{D}_{2} (because for D<D^2D<\hat{D}_{2}, s​o​l1,2sol_{1,2} are not real or both strictly negative and also for D<D^D<\hat{D} no Turing instability can appear).

We now can perform a qualitative study of the behaviour of the roots s​o​l1,2​(D)sol_{1,2}(D), when we let the parameter D>D^2D>\hat{D}_{2} vary. In particular, we have that, from (97),

∀D>D^2,s​o​l1,2​(D)>0.\forall D>\hat{D}_{2},\qquad sol_{1,2}(D)>0.

Moreover, again from formula (97), it can easily be seen that

s​o​l1​(D^2)=s​o​l2​(D^2)=D1​J22∗+D^2​J11∗2​D1​D^2>0,sol_{1}(\hat{D}_{2})=sol_{2}(\hat{D}_{2})=\dfrac{D_{1}J^{*}_{22}+\hat{D}_{2}J^{*}_{11}}{2D_{1}\hat{D}_{2}}>0,

limD→+∞s​o​l2​(D)=J11∗D1>s​o​l2​(D^2),\displaystyle{\lim_{D\to+\infty}}{sol_{2}(D)}=\dfrac{J^{*}_{11}}{D_{1}}>sol_{2}(\hat{D}_{2}),

and

limD→+∞s​o​l1​(D)=0.\displaystyle{\lim_{D\to+\infty}}{sol_{1}(D)}=0.

Furthermore, differentiating (97) with respect to DD, we obtain

∂∂D​s​o​l2​(D)=−J22∗2​D2+1D2​−J∗12J∗21det𝑱∗​[J22∗2​D1​J22∗+D​J11∗D1​D+det𝑱∗D1​D2],\dfrac{\partial}{\partial D}sol_{2}(D)=-\dfrac{J^{*}_{22}}{2D^{2}}+\dfrac{1}{D^{2}\sqrt{-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21}\det\bm{J}^{*}}}\left[\dfrac{J^{*}_{22}}{2}\dfrac{D_{1}J^{*}_{22}+DJ^{*}_{11}}{D_{1}D}+\dfrac{\det\bm{J}^{*}}{D_{1}D^{2}}\right],

and

∂∂D​s​o​l1​(D)=14​D3​D1​1−J∗12J∗21det𝑱​[J22∗​s​o​l1​(D)−2​D​det𝑱∗],\dfrac{\partial}{\partial D}sol_{1}(D)=\dfrac{1}{4D^{3}D_{1}}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{-J^{*}_{12}J^{*}_{21}\det\bm{J}}}\left[J^{*}_{22}sol_{1}(D)-2D\det\bm{J}^{*}\right],

This means that the value of s​o​l1sol_{1} is strictly increasing with respect to DD, while the value of s​o​l2sol_{2} is strictly decreasing. Then, we see that the Turing instability region grows for larger values of DD. Because of this, the choice of a diffusion rate based only on the behaviour of searching predators would lead to inaccurate conclusions about the possibility of pattern formation.

We then compare the Turing instability regions in the cases 2 and 3, that is when the characteristic matrices are

𝑴L​P=[J11∗−D1​λkJ12∗J21∗J22∗−DP​λk],\bm{M}_{LP}=\begin{bmatrix}J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{12}\\[5.69046pt] J^{*}_{21}&J^{*}_{22}-D_{P}\lambda_{k}\end{bmatrix},

and

𝑴L​P=[J11∗−D1​λkJ12∗J21∗−JΔ​21∗​λkJ22∗−JΔ​22∗​λk].\bm{M}_{LP}=\begin{bmatrix}J^{*}_{11}-D_{1}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{12}\\[5.69046pt] J^{*}_{21}-J^{*}_{\Delta 21}\lambda_{k}&J^{*}_{22}-J^{*}_{\Delta 22}\lambda_{k}\end{bmatrix}.

Those coefficients write:

AL\displaystyle A_{L} :=D1​DP,\displaystyle:=D_{1}D_{P}, BL:=DP​J11∗+D1​J22∗,\displaystyle B_{L}:=D_{P}J^{*}_{11}+D_{1}J^{*}_{22},

AL\displaystyle A_{L} =D1​[D2​(1−2​μΓ)+D3​2​μΓ],\displaystyle=D_{1}\left[D_{2}\left(1-\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}\right)+D_{3}\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}\right],

and

D2​(1−2​μΓ)+D3​2​μΓ<D2​(γQ∗+P∗Q∗​(1−2​μΓ))+D3​2​μ​γQ∗​(Γ−2​μ).D_{2}\left(1-\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}\right)+D_{3}\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}<D_{2}\left(\dfrac{\gamma}{Q_{*}}+\dfrac{P_{*}}{Q_{*}}\left(1-\dfrac{2\mu}{\Gamma}\right)\right)+D_{3}\dfrac{2\mu\gamma}{Q_{*}(\Gamma-2\mu)}.

  1. 1.

    There are no regions of strictly negative determinant for both linear and cross diffusion (Figure 1(a)).

  2. 2.

    The linear diffusion case has a Turing instability region, but the determinant of the cross diffusion case is positive for all λk\lambda_{k} (Figure 1(b)), so that the cross diffusion case does not lead to Turing instability.

  3. 3.

    Both cases lead to nonempty Turing instability regions (Figure 1(c)) and we check that

    BL2−4​A1​detJ∗2​AL>BC2−4​AC​detJ∗2​AC,\dfrac{\sqrt{B_{L}^{2}-4A_{1}\det J_{*}}}{2A_{L}}>\dfrac{\sqrt{B_{C}^{2}-4A_{C}\det J_{*}}}{2A_{C}},

    which means that the Turing instability region for the cross diffusion case is strictly included in the Turing instability region of the linear diffusion case.

In all cases, we see that the use of the cross-diffusion model leads to a possibility of obtaining nontrivial patterns which is less likely than when the linear diffusion model is considered. Therefore, the use of a model in which standard diffusion terms are directly added to the reaction terms may lead to an overestimate of the set of the parameters for which patterns appear.

4 Concluding remarks

This paper focuses on the study of two “microscopic” (in terms of time scales) predator-prey models with diffusion, that enable to recover, in a suitable limit, two classical functional responses in the reaction part of the equations and contain a cross-diffusion term. We have also presented rigorous results of convergence of the solutions of these systems towards the solution of the limiting reaction-cross diffusion system.

We first start with two trophic levels, prey and predators, which are further divided into searching predators and handling predators. The former are predators active in the predation process, the latter are resting individuals. Then, we start from a system of three partial differential equations, with standard diffusion terms (a constant times the Laplacian), and with a Lotka-Volterra reaction term. Through a quasi steady-state approximation, we end up with a system of two PDEs with prey and total predator densities as unknowns, in which a Holling-type II functional response appears together with a cross-diffusion term in the predator equation. This means that the diffusion term relative to predators is much more complicated than a constant times Laplacian of PP (linear diffusive term), which in some other models is simply added to the reaction part [39]. In particular, the diffusion term obtained in this way depends on the prey biomass and on both the diffusion coefficients of searching and handling predators d2d_{2} and d3d_{3}. Looking at its expression, the cross-diffusion term reduces the predator diffusion when the prey density increases.

Then we modify the starting model by inserting a competition among predators. With this change we end up after a quasi steady-state approximation with a system of two PDEs for prey and total predator densities, characterized by a Beddington-DeAngelis-like functional response, and a cross-diffusion term in the predator equation.

Also in this case, the limiting system presents a cross-diffusion in the predator equation, which depends on both the diffusion coefficients of searching and handling predators d2d_{2} and d3d_{3}.

The Turing instability analysis of the limiting equations is studied in Chapter 3. For the first one, it is known that predator-prey models with a prey-dependent trophic function in the reaction part and (standard) linear-diffusion cannot give rise to Turing instability [9]. Even with the cross-diffusion model, no patterns seem to appear under a (biologically reasonable) assumption on the diffusion coefficients. For the second system, in which a Beddington-DeAngelis-like functional response appears, we look for conditions on the parameter values which lead to Turing instability and we compare these Turing instability regions with the ones obtained when the cross-diffusion term is substituted by a standard diffusion. The main point is the fact that the Turing instability region associated to the cross-diffusion system is always strictly included in the Turing instability region of the linear-diffusion system. As a consequence, the use of reaction-diffusion systems for predator-prey interactions of Beddington-DeAngelis type in which standard diffusion is simply added to the reaction terms may lead to an overestimate of the possibility of appearance of patterns (at least in the case when the Beddington-DeAngelis functional response is a consequence of the interactions between searching and handling predators).

It is worth mentioning that in many instances, the introduction of cross-diffusion terms instead of (standard) linear-diffusion terms leads exactly to the opposite result, that is, the increase of the set of parameter values in which patterns develop [32, 33, 40]. Our study leads then to a rather interesting conclusion: pattern formation originating from Turing instability is counteracted by the cross-diffusion term derived by the Quasi-Steady State Approximation.
